paper_title: FlyHash for LLM Agent Memory: An Empirical Validation and a New Application

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly rely on external memory stores to retain information across conversations, typically via dense vector embeddings searched with approximate nearest-neighbor methods. The fruit fly's olfactory circuit computes a locality-sensitive hash of sensory input using a strikingly different mechanism - sparse random projection followed by winner-take-all competition - and prior work (Dasgupta et al., 2017) showed this scheme, dubbed FlyHash, preserves neighbor structure better per bit than conventional random-hyperplane hashing (SimHash) on several benchmarks. We apply FlyHash, to our knowledge for the first time, to LLM agent memory retrieval, and ask three questions a practitioner actually needs answered: does the quality advantage hold under a correctly matched-bit protocol (it does, robustly, across 10 seeds and four datasets spanning two modalities, with one specific, previously undocumented comparison pitfall identified and corrected along the way); does that advantage translate into real memory and latency savings, including against the dense-vector indexing (HNSW) practitioners default to today (no: at equal bits FlyHash's codes are larger and slower to compare than SimHash's, and HNSW dominates both hash methods at ordinary scale; a sparse-set comparison we introduce recovers most but not all of a naive latency gap, leaving hashing's practical case narrower and more specific than the quality result alone implies); and does the advantage survive genuine, non-circular agent-memory relevance labels rather than the nearest-neighbor-by-embedding proxy this literature otherwise relies on (it does). We report all three answers precisely, including the two that narrow rather than flatter the headline result, and release our implementation, a working agent-memory demo, and a full account of the methodological pitfalls we found and corrected.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Large language model agents that operate over long or repeated interactions increasingly need memory: way to store facts, preferences, or prior context and retrieve the relevant pieces on demand (Chhikara et al., 2025). The dominant approach embeds each memory as dense vector and retrieves by approximate nearest-neighbor search over an index such as FAISS (Johnson et al., 2021; see also the RAG survey of Zhao et al., 2024), though hybrid retrieval architectures combining dense and lexical signals are an active and growing alternative. This works well but scales in memory and compute with the size and dimensionality of the stored embeddings, motivating interest in more Code: https://github.com/mohanji/flyhash-agent-memory Archive (DOI): https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23903302 1 compact representations in particular, hashing schemes that compress an embedding into short binary code while preserving enough neighbor structure to remain useful for retrieval. One such scheme, introduced by Dasgupta, Stevens, and Navlakha (2017) and directly inspired by neurobiology, computes locality-sensitive hash the way the fruit flys olfactory circuit is believed to encode odors: roughly 50 receptor-neuron activations are randomly and sparsely projected into approximately 2,000 Kenyon cells, of which only the top 5% most active are allowed to fire, producing sparse binary code. The original paper showed that this scheme which we refer to as FlyHash, following subsequent literature preserves nearest-neighbor structure better, at matched number of output bits, than SimHash (Charikar, 2002), the standard random-hyperplane hashing baseline, on several benchmark datasets including SIFT, GloVe, and MNIST. Despite this result and several follow-up papers extending the algorithm (surveyed in Section 2), we are not aware of any prior work applying FlyHash-style hashing specifically to LLM agent memory retrieval setting that is, in several respects, natural fit: agent memories are frequently decomposed into short, numerous, semantically embedded units retrieved by similarity (Hu et al., 2026; Du, 2026; Zeng et al., 2024) the regime this papers evaluation targets, though we note that recent work increasingly favors structured or hierarchical retrieval over flat similarity search for longer-horizon tasks (Cao et al., 2026; Hu et al., 2026). This paper is organized around three research questions, each answered precisely rather than in the aggregate, because as we show below the answers are not all the same shape: RQ1. Under protocol that correctly holds FlyHashs and SimHashs active bit counts equal (Section 3.2), does FlyHashs reported per-bit retrieval-quality advantage over SimHash hold for data representative of LLM agent memory, robustly across seeds and datasets? (Sections 4.14.2; answer: yes, with one specific, previously undocumented comparison pitfall that must be avoided to get there Appendix A.) RQ2. Does that quality advantage translate into an actual resource advantage lower memory, lower query latency in realistic deployment, including against the dense-vector indexing methods (HNSW) practitioners use by default today? (Sections 4.34.4, 4.6; answer: not by default, and not relative to HNSW at ordinary scale hashings resource case is narrower than the quality result alone would suggest.) RQ3. Does the quality advantage hold under genuine, non-circular agent-memory relevance labels, rather than the nearest-neighbor-by-embedding proxy used everywhere else in this literature (including the original FlyHash paper)? (Section 4.7; answer: yes.) In service of these questions, the papers contributions are: (1) the first application, to our knowledge, of FlyHash to LLM agent memory retrieval, with working end-to-end system (Sections 3.5, 4.5); (2) the matched-active-bit protocol itself, stated precisely enough to prevent specific conflation we discovered by reproducing discrepancy with published result (Section 3.2, Appendix A); (3) statistical and cross-dataset validation beyond the original paper 10 seeds, four datasets across two modalities, 36-configuration hyperparameter sweep, and paired statistical analysis (Sections 4.14.2); and (4) an honest, multi-angle resource and deployment analysis that does not stop at the quality result brute-force memory/latency costs, sparse-set comparison, direct HNSW systems baseline, and relevance-label upgrade (Sections 4.34.4, 4.64.7). The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 situates this work relative to FlyHashs original paper and its algorithmic follow-ups. Section 3 describes the method, evaluation protocol, datasets, and statistical procedure. Section 4 presents results. Section 5 discusses their implications. Section 6 states limitations and future work. Appendix gives full account of the reproducibility investigation that motivated the corrected protocol in Section 3.2.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: The original algorithm. Dasgupta, Stevens, and Navlakha (2017) introduced the algorithm this paper builds on, showing that neurally-plausible circuit sparse random projection into much higher-dimensional space, followed by winner-take-all sparsification functions as localitysensitive hash competitive with, and often superior to, dense random-hyperplane hashing (SimHash; Charikar, 2002) at matched number of output bits. Their evaluation covered SIFT descriptors, GloVe word vectors, and MNIST images. This paper directly reuses their algorithm and their choice of evaluation datasets (GloVe and MNIST; we do not evaluate on SIFT see Section 6), applying it to problem domain they did not consider. DenseFly. Sharma and Navlakha (2018) extended the base algorithm with DenseFly, which densifies FlyHashs sparse output as post-processing step to further improve similarity search accuracy. This is genuine algorithmic improvement over plain FlyHash that we do not implement here; we discuss it as natural future work in Section 6. BioHash. Ryali, Hopfield, Grinberg, and Krotov (2020) replaced FlyHashs random sparse projection with learned one, trained with biologically-plausible local learning rule, and reported improved retrieval accuracy over the random-projection version across several datasets. Their paper also established mean Average Precision (mAP) as the standard evaluation metric for this line of work, which we adopt in Section 3.2. We note for transparency that BioHashs learned projection is reported to outperform the plain FlyHash evaluated in this paper; our contribution is not better hash function, but an application and validation of the simpler, random-projection version, which requires no training data or learning procedure practically relevant trade-off for lightweight agent-memory component. FlyNN. Most recently, work applying the fly olfactory circuit to federated nearest-neighbor classification (FlyNN, AAAI 2022) illustrates the breadth of problems this biological mechanism has been adapted to beyond pure hashing, extending it to federated learning setting. Existing implementations. general-purpose FlyHash package is available on PyPI (Huang, MIT license), providing NumPy-compatible implementation of the base algorithm for small-tomedium input dimensionalities. Its existence confirms that an implementation of the algorithm itself is not novel contribution; our implementation exists to support the specific experiments in this paper rather than to serve as general-purpose library. Graph-based approximate nearest-neighbor search. different line of work achieves fast approximate retrieval not by compressing each vector into short code, but by building navigable graph over the full-precision (or lightly quantized) vectors and searching it via greedy graph traversal. HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World graphs; Malkov and Yashunin, 2016/2020) is the dominant practical method in this family and underlies most production vector-search systems in use today (e.g., FAISSs IndexHNSW, and the default indexes in several vector databases including Milvus, Pinecone, Weaviate, and pgvector; Idrees et al., 2026). HNSW and hashing schemes like FlyHash and SimHash target different points in the retrieval design space: HNSW optimizes for sublinear query time and high recall at the cost of storing richer per-item structure (full or near-full vectors plus graph edges), while FlyHash and SimHash optimize for extreme per-record compactness short binary code compared via cheap Hamming distance at the cost of the brute-force, linear-scan comparison this paper evaluates throughout. Our main results (Sections 4.14.4) isolate hashing-function quality by comparing FlyHash against SimHash at matched bit budgets, rather than against HNSW, since the two are different design points (compact-code quality versus indexed graph search); we separately report direct, explicitly-labeled systems comparison against HNSW in Section 4 for readers asking the practical which would actually deploy question. LLM memory architectures and retrieval-augmented generation. large and rapidly 3 growing body of work designs memory systems for LLM agents directly, distinct from the hashingalgorithm literature surveyed above: production-oriented long-term memory frameworks (Chhikara et al., 2025), structural memory representations spanning chunks, triples, and summaries (Zeng et al., 2024), and recent surveys of agent memory mechanisms and evaluation (Du, 2026). This literatures central recent finding that flat, independent similarity retrieval over text snippets can suffer from redundancy and relational blindness at longer horizons, motivating structured or hierarchical retrieval instead (Hu et al., 2026; Cao et al., 2026) is complementary to this papers contribution: we evaluate hashing methods within the flat similarity-based retrieval regime that remains widely used baseline (e.g., Mem0-style systems), rather than proposing or evaluating structured memory architecture; combining FlyHash-style hashing with structured retrieval is natural future work (Section 6). Vector quantization and alternative hashing families. separate line of work compresses dense vectors via quantization rather than binary hashing. Product Quantization (Jegou, Douze, & Schmid, 2010) and its optimized variants (Ge et al., 2013) achieve higher retrieval accuracy than binary hashing at comparable memory budgets by preserving continuous distance estimates via asymmetric lookup tables rather than collapsing to Hamming codes; recent methods such as RaBitQ extend this advantage to extreme, 1-bit-per-dimension compression (Gao & Long, 2024). We do not evaluate against this family here, since our focus is head-to-head comparison between two hashing paradigms under matched-bit protocol, but it represents stronger baseline than either hash method at most operating points consistent with the HNSW result in Section 4.6. Within the hashing family itself, more sophisticated locality-sensitive schemes such as Cross-Polytope LSH achieve better asymptotic query exponent than random-hyperplane hashing (Laarhoven, 2020), but this advantage only materializes at large scale and high ambient dimension; at the moderate dataset sizes evaluated here  (Table 1)  , hyperplane-based SimHash remains competitive or superior in wall-clock performance due to lower per-hash computational overhead (Cai, 2016; Laarhoven, 2020), motivating our choice of standard SimHash, rather than Cross-Polytope LSH, as the baseline. Sparse lexical retrieval. different line of sparse retrieval work BM25, and learned sparse lexical models such as SPLADE (Formal, Lassance, Piwowarski, & Clinchant, 2024) operates directly on text via sparse term-weight vectors over vocabulary, which is distinct notion of sparsity from the sparse binary codes FlyHash derives from dense embeddings via winner-take-all competition. These lexical methods are complementary, not competing, approach, well-suited to exact keyword matching rather than semantic similarity over learned embeddings, and are outside this papers scope of embedding-based hashing methods. This papers position. None of the above apply FlyHash-style hashing to LLM agent memory retrieval, and none report the depth of statistical validation (multi-seed variance, multi-dataset, multi-modality, hyperparameter ablation) presented in Section 4. The gap this paper fills is at the intersection of new, currently relevant application and level of empirical rigor including documented and corrected methodological pitfall that the base algorithms literature does not yet provide.

sections.title: 3.1 FlyHash and SimHash
sections.content: Both hashing schemes take dense input vector Rd and produce binary output code. SimHash (Charikar, 2002) draws dense random matrix Rkd with entries sampled i.i.d. 4 from standard normal distribution, and outputs hsim(x) = sign(W x) {0, 1}k. Every one of the output bits is thresholded independently; the code is dense in the sense that each bit is set to 1 with probability approximately 1/2. FlyHash (Dasgupta et al., 2017) instead draws sparse random projection matrix Rmd, where each row (each Kenyon cell) is connected to only random subset of sd input dimensions (s is the sparsity, fixed at 0.10 throughout this paper, following the flys own connectivity, where each Kenyon cell integrates inputs from roughly 512% of input channels; Caron, Ruta, Abbott, & Axel, 2013), with weights drawn uniformly from {1, +1} on those connections and zero elsewhere. The projection is then passed through k-winners-take-all operation: only the largest of the projected values are set to 1, all others to 0: hfly(x) = WTAk(P x) {0, 1}m, hfly(x)0 = k. We refer to as the pool size (the total number of Kenyon cells, fixed at 2,000 in our experiments unless otherwise stated) and as the bit budget (the number of winning, active bits). This notational distinction versus is deliberately explicit, because conflating the two is the source of the reproducibility discrepancy described in Section 3.2 and Appendix A.

sections.title: 3.2 Evaluation protocol
sections.content: Metric. Following BioHash (Ryali et al., 2020), we evaluate retrieval quality with mean Average Precision at (mAP@R). For query q, let the relevant set be its true nearest neighbors under exact Euclidean distance on the original (unhashed) embeddings. Average Precision for is AP(q) = 1 (cid:88) ℓ=1 Precision(ℓ) Rel(ℓ), where Rel(ℓ) = 1 if the item ranked ℓ-th by Hamming distance under the hash code is in the relevant set, and Precision(ℓ) is the fraction of relevant items among the top ℓ ranked results. mAP@R is the mean of AP(q) over all queries. Unlike plain recall@k, mAP@R rewards ranking true neighbors earlier, not merely including them somewhere in the top R. Matched-active-bit (quality-per-active-bit) protocol. The central methodological point of this paper concerns what it means to compare FlyHash and SimHash at the same number of bits. There are at least three distinct, non-interchangeable notions of parity one could hold fixed: 1. Equal active/output bits the number of bits that are actually compared by Hamming distance per query (k for both methods). This is the notion we use throughout Sections 4.1 4.2, and we call it the matched-active-bit protocol to avoid the vaguer, overloaded term fair comparison. 2. Equal physical storage the number of bytes each methods code occupies at rest, which depends on representation (dense vs. packed vs. sparse-index), not just (Sections 4.34.4). 3. Equal query-time/resource budget the number of bytes moved or compared per query, which can differ from storage when methods on-disk and in-memory representations differ (Sections 4.34.4, 4.6). Conflating these is the specific pitfall this paper is built around. Concretely, under the matchedactive-bit protocol, for each bit budget we evaluate FlyHash with pool size fixed at large value (2,000, unless stated otherwise) and the winner-take-all fraction set to k/m, and we evaluate SimHash with exactly output bits so both methods produce the same number of active bits, isolating the quality of the hash function from either methods absolute output size. This is not the naive way to run the comparison: naive implementation might instead fix FlyHashs total output width (i.e., set to whatever bits value is being swept) and hold the winner-take-all percentage fixed (e.g., 5%, matching the flys own biology) in which case FlyHashs effective number of active bits at given nominal bits value is only small fraction of that value, while SimHash is given the full nominal count as genuinely active bits. This conflation of (notion 1) with silently and substantially disadvantages FlyHash, and is distinct from the storage/resource conflations addressed later (notions 2 and 3, Sections 4.34.4). We discovered the first pitfall by reproducing discrepancy with published result; the full diagnostic process, including hypotheses we initially pursued and later ruled out, is given in Appendix A.

sections.title: 3.4 Statistical protocol
sections.content: Both FlyHashs sparse projection matrix and SimHashs dense hyperplane matrix are randomly initialized, so single evaluation reflects one particular random draw, not the expected behavior of the method. For our main results (Section 4.1) and hyperparameter ablation (Section 4.2), we repeat every evaluation across independent random seeds (10 for the main results, 3 for the larger hyperparameter sweep, given its greater number of configurations), varying only the projection matrices initialization across seeds while holding the dataset and the sampled set of queries fixed. This isolates projection-matrix randomness as the source of measured variance, rather than conflating it with variance from query sampling. We report the mean and standard deviation of mAP@R across seeds, and, as simple and intentionally conservative robustness check, whether the gap between FlyHashs and SimHashs mean mAP exceeds twice their combined standard deviation ( > 2 sim). We present this as sanity check against attributing an observed gap to projection-matrix noise, not as substitute for formal statistical significance test. fly + σ2 σ2 (cid:113) Because FlyHash and SimHash are evaluated on the same 10 seeds (same sampled queries, same train/query split, differing only in which methods projection matrix that seed initializes), the two methods mAP values at given bit budget are naturally paired, not independent samples each seed contributes one paired difference di = mAPfly,i mAPsim,i. For our primary GloVe result (the first block of Table 2, and Table 3 below) we additionally report paired analysis: the mean paired difference with both t-interval and bootstrap (10,000 resamples) 95% confidence interval, the paired effect size (Cohens dz), and two nonparametric tests that do not assume normality the Wilcoxon signed-rank test and sign-flip permutation test (10,000 permutations). This is strictly stronger statement than the robust heuristic above, which compares marginal variances and discards the pairing.

sections.title: 3.5 Agent memory integration
sections.content: To validate the practical use case motivating this work, we implement minimal LLM agent memory system: plain text remember(text) / recall(query, k) interface wraps sentence-transformer embedding model and FlyHash-backed store, so that an agent interacts only with text, not embeddings or hash codes directly. We wire this into live tool-use loop with general-purpose LLM exposing two tools save memory, called when the model judges the user has shared fact worth remembering, and recall memory, called when answering question that may depend on previously shared fact. In representative interaction, user states two facts in one turn (My favorite language is Python and Im allergic to peanuts), asks an unrelated question in the next turn, and then asks What should avoid eating? in third turn; the agent correctly answers peanuts by calling recall memory, retrieving the relevant fact via FlyHash-based Hammingdistance ranking over stored memory embeddings from several turns earlier. This demonstrates the full pipeline functioning end-to-end, independent of the benchmark-style evaluation in Section 4.

sections.title: 4.4 A sparse-set comparison: partial recovery
sections.content: Because every FlyHash code has exactly active bits, the Hamming distance between two such codes reduces to 2k 2AB, where and are their sets of active indices. Ranking by Hamming distance is therefore identical to ranking by descending intersection size, which we compute as sparse-sparse matrix product over only the active indices, rather than dense operation over the full m-wide array. 10 Figure 2: FlyHash mAP@100 across the sparsity pool-size grid, at = 16, 64, 256. Each panels SimHash baseline is given in its title; every cell in every panel is above that baseline. The rightward brightening within the = 256 panel visualizes the pool-size effect, and the top-to-bottom brightening within each panel visualizes the sparsity effect. Table 6: Sparse vs. dense FlyHash comparison, and memory as an explicit index list (uint16 per active index). (bits) Sparse-idx bytes/rec 16 32 64 128 256 32 64 128 256 512 SimHash SimHash bytes/rec ms/query ms/query ms/query Sparse Dense 2 4 8 16 15.77 14.44 14.54 15.03 13.90 0.71 0.73 1.59 3.39 8.55 0.40 0.29 0.45 0.84 1.79 The sparse comparison is 1022 faster than the dense comparison and, unlike the dense version, its latency correctly scales with rather than remaining flat. It does not, however, close the gap to SimHash entirely: SimHashs small dense matrix multiplication remains 25 faster at every budget tested, and explicit index-list storage, while now also correctly scaling with k, remains 16 larger than SimHashs bit-packed code, since storing an explicit position costs full integer where bit-packing costs single bit. We report this as genuine, partial improvement not solved problem and discuss the remaining gap in Section 6.

sections.title: 4.5 Agent memory demonstration
sections.content: in the representative interThe end-to-end system described in Section 3.5 functions correctly: action described there, the agent retrieves fact shared several turns earlier via FlyHash-based Hamming ranking over MiniLM sentence embeddings, without that fact appearing anywhere in the immediate conversational context. This confirms the pipeline is functional for its intended use case, independent of the benchmark numbers in Sections 4.14.4. As one measured data point for the full pipelines latency (embedding included, not just the isolated hash comparison of Sections 4.34.4), we timed single representative query against the 6,000-record corpus of Section 4.7, averaged over 30 repeats on consumer hardware, using the sparse-set comparison method of Section 4.4 for the hash-ranking step (the same method behind Table 6s speed numbers, consistent with the rest of the paper rather than an unrelated, unoptimized implementation): 11 Table 7: End-to-end pipeline latency, one representative query (30 repeats). Stage ms/query % of total Sentence embedding (MiniLM) FlyHash hash + sparse rank Total end-to-end 14.1 6.4 20.5 68.8% 31.2% 100% With the hash-ranking step measured consistently with Table 6, sentence embedding not FlyHashs hash comparison is the dominant cost of the full pipeline, by roughly 2:1. This is useful finding in its own right: it means that, at this corpus size, FlyHashs own contribution to end-to-end latency is modest relative to the (hash-independent) embedding step, and that further latency optimization in real deployment would pay off more from the embedding stage than the hash comparison. Embedding time is identical regardless of which hash is used downstream, so this number has no bearing on the FlyHash-vs-SimHash comparisons elsewhere in the paper it exists only to put real figure on the full pipelines latency rather than leaving it unmeasured. We still report it as single data point on one machine, not benchmark: no seed averaging and no variation in corpus size or hardware. proper system-level benchmark remains future work (Section 6).

sections.title: 4.6 Practical systems comparison: FlyHash/SimHash vs. a graph-based ANN
sections.content: index Sections 4.14.4 hold the active-bit budget fixed and compare FlyHash against SimHash both compact hash codes compared by Hamming distance. This answers which hash is better at given bit budget, but not would actually use either of these instead of standard production ANN index. We report that second, separate question here using FAISSs IndexHNSWFlat (M = 32, efConstruction= 200) over full-precision GloVe vectors (5,000 records, 50 queries, mAP@100), explicitly as systems comparison rather than matched-bit one: HNSW has no bits parameter comparable to k, so its quality/speed/memory trade-off is governed by efSearch instead, and the two tables below should be read within themselves, not row-matched against each other. (bits) FlyHash mAP FlyHash ms/q FlyHash B/rec SimHash mAP SimHash ms/q 16 32 64 128 256 0.198 0.312 0.440 0.582 0.697 0.66 1.04 1.62 4.46 10.13 0.048 0.095 0.185 0.325 0.476 0.19 0.22 0.26 0.50 0.70 32 64 128 256 12 At this scale, HNSW dominates both hash methods on quality and latency simultaneously mAP above 0.98 and sub-0.1ms queries, at only 1.6 the raw exact-storage memory cost (671.5 vs. 400 bytes/record) while FlyHash and SimHashs only genuine advantage is extreme compactness well below exact storage (as little as 232 bytes/record). The honest conclusion is that practitioner with no unusual memory constraint and dataset at this scale should use HNSW, not hash code; FlyHash/SimHashs relevance is specifically to the regime HNSW does not target severe, explicit storage budgets (e.g., many independent memory stores on resource-constrained agents) and we revise our framing in Section 5 accordingly rather than letting Sections 4.14.4 imply general retrieval recommendation.

sections.title: 4.7 A realistic, labeled agent-memory benchmark
sections.content: Every result above uses nearest-neighbor-by-embedding as stand-in for relevance two items are treated as relevant to each other if an unhashed embedding considers them close, which is circular with respect to the embedding itself and does not test anything about whether hashing preserves true query-to-memory relevance. We address this with separate benchmark using constructed relevance labels that do not derive from any embedding distance. Established agent-memory benchmarks such as LoCoMo (Maharana et al., 2024) and LongMemEval (Wu et al., 2024) evaluate end-to-end conversational QA accuracy over multi-session dialogue, which conflates retrieval quality with the downstream LLMs reasoning over retrieved context (Wu et al., 2024, explicitly separate indexing, retrieval, and reading for this reason). Our evaluation instead requires ground-truth relevance labels for the retrieval step in isolation the quantity FlyHash and SimHash actually compete on which these QA-style benchmarks do not provide directly. We therefore construct dataset with explicit, non-circular relevance labels anchored to named personas below, in the same spirit as recent calls for benchmark designs that disentangle retrieval correctness from answer correctness (Wu et al., 2024; Hao et al., 2026). Construction. We generate 150 synthetic named personas, each with 10 independent facts (favorite color, allergy, job title, hometown, and six others), each fact expressed via 34 paraphrase templates that name the persona directly (e.g., Jordans favorite color is teal. / If you ask Jordan, teal is their favorite color.), giving 6,000 memory sentences total. Each query is differently-worded question that also names target persona (e.g., Which color does Jordan like best?), and its ground-truth relevant set is exactly that personas own paraphrases for that fact (34 sentences out of 6,000) label fixed by construction, not by embedding similarity. Naming every fact and question to specific persona is what makes the corpus both genuinely confusable (thousands of near-identical same-template statements about other people crowd every query) and answerable from text content alone (the one token that correctly disambiguates the right answer the name is actually present in the query), which an earlier, unnamed version of this design was not: without persona name tying question to answer, no text-similarity method, hashed or not, can identify whose stated value is correct among many textually identical same-template statements, and we do not report numbers from that earlier, ill-posed version. Embedding. We embed both memories and queries with TF-IDF followed by truncated SVD (256 components), fit on the memory corpus an offline, network-free stand-in for real sentencetransformer embedding, consistent with this projects practice elsewhere (Section 6). FlyHash beats SimHash robustly at every budget on this genuinely-labeled task, with absolute mAP values well above chance (random ranking over 6,000 items with 4 relevant would score far below 0.1) but, expectedly, lower than Table 2s nearest-neighbor-pseudo-label mAP this is harder, more realistic task by construction, and the two numbers are not meant to be compared directly. This result is, to our knowledge, the first time FlyHashs advantage over SimHash has Table 10: FlyHash vs. SimHash, standard mean Average Precision against constructed relevance labels (150 queries, 6,000 memories, 10 seeds). sections.title: 5 Discussion
sections.content: Why is the advantage largest at low bit budgets? FlyHashs sparse expansion into much higher-dimensional space before selecting winners appears to preserve more of the inputs neighborhood structure per output bit than SimHashs direct dense projection, particularly when very few bits are available to encode that structure. As the bit budget grows, both methods have enough capacity to represent more of the relevant structure, and the relative gap narrows though FlyHashs absolute advantage never disappears across any budget we tested  (Table 2)  . This pattern is practically significant: real deployments of compact hashing are motivated precisely by wanting few bits per record (that is the entire point of hashing over storing full embeddings), so the regime where FlyHashs advantage is largest is also the regime real system would actually operate in. quality advantage is not automatically resource advantage. Section 4.3 is, to our knowledge, an underappreciated point in this line of work: hash function can preserve neighbor structure strictly better than baseline while, in naive implementation, being simultaneously worse on memory and speed because better structure per bit and cheap to store and compare are different properties that do not automatically follow from each other. Section 4.4 shows that principled fix targeting the comparisons sparsity recovers much, but not all, of one axis (speed) while leaving the other (memory) only partially improved. We think this distinction qualityper-bit versus deployed resource cost is worth making explicit in any evaluation of hashing scheme derived from sparse-coding argument, not only in this paper. Practical implication for agent memory. An agent adopting FlyHash today obtains genuine, robustly validated retrieval-quality improvement per bit over SimHash, particularly in the low-bit-budget regime most relevant to resource-constrained memory system, and (Section 4.7) that advantage survives contact with genuine, non-circular relevance labels, not just an embeddingsimilarity proxy. It should not, on the basis of this paper, expect memory or latency improvement over well-implemented SimHash baseline without further engineering (Section 6), nor should it expect either hash method to beat standard production ANN index such as HNSW at ordinary scale (Section 4.6) HNSW wins on quality and latency simultaneously there, at modest memory premium over exact storage. Which of these properties matters most depends on the deployment: system already committed to compact hash codes, bottlenecked on retrieval accuracy at fixed, small bit budget, benefits from FlyHash as drop-in SimHash replacement; system with no unusual storage constraint should likely use HNSW instead of either hash; and system bottlenecked specifically on raw per-record storage at scale where even HNSWs overhead is unaffordable is the narrow regime where FlyHash/SimHash-style hashing is the right tool at all.

sections.title: 6 Limitations and Future Work
sections.content: Memory and speed do not fully match the quality advantage, even after targeted attempt to close the gap. Section 4.4s sparse-set comparison recovers most of the speed disadvantage but leaves meaningful memory disadvantage; genuinely sublinear index (e.g., banded or multi-probe LSH, or an inverted index verified sublinear at scale an earlier invertedindex attempt in our own implementation was found not to be sublinear at the scales we tested) remains unbuilt. more compact encoding of the active-index list (delta-coding of sorted indices, variable-length or entropy coding, or reducing pool size at some cost to quality) is concrete, identified next step we did not pursue here. Our HNSW comparison (Section 4.6) is single-scale, single-configuration snapshot. We report one dataset (GloVe, 5,000 records) and one HNSW configuration (M = 32, efConstruction= 200, three efSearch values); HNSWs relative advantage over hashing shrinks as per-record storage budgets tighten and may shrink or reverse at very different corpus scales, which we have not swept. combined approach (e.g., FlyHash codes as cheap pre-filter ahead of an HNSW-indexed re-ranking stage, in the spirit of how FAISS combines quantization with HNSW) is natural direction we have not explored. SIFT1M, part of the original papers evaluation, is not included. We judged that four independent datasets across two modalities already provide strong evidence the result is not dataset-specific, and that fifth, necessarily subsampled dataset (SIFT1Ms full 1M-vector scale is impractical to evaluate exhaustively at our compute budget) would add breadth rather than materially new evidence. We report this as deliberate scope decision, not an oversight. We do not implement DenseFlys densification or BioHashs learned projection, both of which are reported improvements over the plain, random-projection FlyHash evaluated here (Section 2). Combining either with the agent-memory application is natural future work. We compare two hashing paradigms (sparse random-projection vs. dense randomhyperplane) but do not benchmark against vector quantization methods (e.g., Product Quantization, RaBitQ), which the literature indicates generally outperform hashing in accuracyper-bit (Jegou et al., 2011; Gao & Long, 2024; Section 2); comparison against quantization is natural future work alongside the HNSW baseline already included. The real-text (MiniLM) evaluation uses small, 100-sentence corpus, chosen to avoid duplicate-embedding artifacts (see Appendix A) rather than to represent realistic agent-memory scale. larger, more diverse real-text corpus would strengthen this specific result. We report only single data point for the full end-to-end agent memory systems latency (Section 4.5: 20.5 ms/query on one machine, one query, 30 repeats), not proper benchmark no seed averaging and no sweep over corpus size or hardware. dedicated, multiseed system-level benchmark is future work. The realistic, labeled agent-memory benchmark (Section 4.7) uses templated synthetic text, not naturally-occurring language, and TF-IDF+SVD embedding as stand-in for real sentence-transformer. Real sentence diversity is considerably messier than any fixed template set, and real deployments would more plausibly scope memory retrieval by session or user ID than rely on name mentioned in free text. rerun with real human-written memory logs and real sentence-transformer embedding (on machine with internet access, the 15 same gap already noted for MiniLM/MNIST elsewhere in this paper) would strengthen this specific result.

sections.title: 7 Conclusion
sections.content: Our three research questions have three different shapes of answer, and we state the claim no wider than that. FlyHash beats SimHash at matched active-bit counts, robustly, on every dataset and seed we tested, including under genuine agent-memory relevance labels rather than an embeddingsimilarity proxy (RQ1, RQ3) this is real, well-supported result, and one previously undocumented comparison pitfall (k-vs-m conflation) had to be corrected to see it. But the practical deployment question (RQ2) does not resolve as cleanly: FlyHashs quality advantage over SimHash does not translate into memory or latency advantage under naive comparison, sparse-set comparison closes most but not all of that gap, and standard production index (HNSW) outperforms both hash methods on every axis at ordinary scale, leaving genuinely extreme storage constraints as hashings specific niche rather than general deployment recommendation. We think this validated hash-quality result, corrected methodological pitfall, and resource picture that narrows rather than flatters the headline claim is more useful contribution to reproducible progress here than report that stopped at the first, more flattering result.

sections.title: A Reproducibility Investigation
sections.content: While reproducing the original papers reported result on GloVe word vectors, we initially found FlyHash losing to SimHash on every dataset we tried synthetic clustered embeddings, TFIDF text vectors, real sentence embeddings, and real GloVe vectors directly contradicting the published finding on GloVe. We treated this discrepancy as signal that our comparison, not the algorithm, was most likely at fault, and pursued it systematically rather than accepting or explaining away the contradiction. Hypotheses ruled out. We first tested whether L2-normalizing inputs before hashing affected the result; it did not, meaningfully. We then tested whether using the algorithms exact original weight definition (true binary {0, 1} projection weights, rather than the signed {1, +1} weights we had implemented) affected the result; it did not, and we quantify this claim across all five main bit budgets below rather than resting it on the single seed we checked at the time. We then tested whether our evaluation metric recall@k by overlap, rather than mAP@R was responsible; switching to mAP@R produced the same qualitative picture. Each ruled-out hypothesis narrowed the search space without resolving the discrepancy. Quantifying the weight-mode claim. The it did not, meaningfully judgment above was originally made on single seed. Re-run across all 10 seeds and all five main bit budgets (GloVe), with SimHash included as reference: Both weight modes beat SimHash by wide margin at every budget tested. The signed-vsbinary difference is not zero and grows with (0.004 at = 16 to 0.058 at = 256), so the honest claim is not no difference but small relative to the FlyHash-vs-SimHash effect at every budget we tested, with modest upward trend at higher the main results in Section 4.1 use the signed variant throughout, and this table bounds how much of that result could plausibly be an artifact of that choice. 18 Table 11: Signed vs. binary FlyHash projection weights, GloVe, 10 seeds. (bits) Signed {1, +1} mAP Binary {0, 1} mAP diff SimHash mAP (ref.) 16 32 64 128 256 0.196 0.007 0.314 0.009 0.449 0.008 0.585 0.006 0.705 0.006 0.191 0.005 0.298 0.007 0.421 0.005 0.540 0.005 0.647 0. 0.0042 0.0156 0.0277 0.0449 0.0577 0.047 0.006 0.096 0.009 0.185 0.008 0.316 0.006 0.469 0.007 The actual cause. We resolved the discrepancy by comparing our implementations parameterization directly against third-party reference implementation of the original algorithm (github.com/dataplayer12/Fly-LSH). This revealed that our comparison held FlyHashs total hash dimensionality equal to SimHashs bit count while separately fixing FlyHashs winner-take-all percentage silently making FlyHashs effective number of active bits, at any given nominal bits value, small fraction of what SimHash was being given as its full, genuinely active bit count. This is precisely the k-versus-m conflation described in Section 3.2. Correcting the protocol to hold (not m) equal between the two methods, with fixed independently at large value, immediately reproduced the original papers reported pattern: FlyHash winning decisively on GloVe at every bit budget, and as it turned out on every other dataset we subsequently tested as well (Section 4.1). hypothesis retracted. Prior to finding this cause, we had observed that FlyHash appeared to outperform SimHash specifically on data with correlated, non-negative features (e.g., TF-IDF text vectors) but not on isotropic synthetic data, and had proposed that FlyHash specifically benefits from such data properties. Once the actual comparison bug was corrected, this pattern disappeared: FlyHash outperformed SimHash on the corrected synthetic isotropic data just as decisively as on text data. We state plainly that our earlier hypothesis was incorrect it was constructed to explain an artifact of flawed comparison, not genuine property of either the data or the algorithm and we retract it here rather than omit it from this account. We document this investigation in this level of detail because the underlying pitfall conflating hashs effective bit count with its nominal parameter dimensionality seems easy to make and is, to our knowledge, not explicitly warned against elsewhere in this literature. We hope stating it precisely, alongside the specific hypotheses that seemed plausible but were not the actual cause, helps others attempting similar comparison avoid the same error.
